common_name: Equestris Moth Orchid (Dwarf Moth Orchid, Horse's Phalaenopsis)

planting.note: Pot in a fine-grade bark or sphagnum mix in a small container that fits the compact root mass; grow as a houseplant on an east window or under lights, since Phalaenopsis equestris cannot tolerate temperatures below 55°F.

directions: Grow in bright, curtain-filtered light with no direct midday sun, in a fine-bark or sphagnum mix that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged. Phalaenopsis equestris is a miniature species from the Philippines and Taiwan that branches readily from old inflorescences, producing a nearly continuous succession of small, 1-inch lavender-pink to white flowers with a darker pink lip throughout the year rather than one seasonal bloom. Its compact size and free-flowering habit have made it one of the most widely used parents in modern miniature and novelty phalaenopsis hybrids. Maintain warm temperatures and moderate humidity year-round, and avoid cutting spent spikes back hard since new branches and flowers often continue to emerge from them.

planting.note: Pot in a coarse, fast-draining bark mix in a wide, shallow container to suit its spreading root system; grow as a houseplant on an east or shaded south window, since Phalaenopsis stuartiana cannot tolerate frost or chilling below 55°F.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a coarse, fast-draining bark mix, watering thoroughly and letting the mix approach dryness at the surface before watering again. Phalaenopsis stuartiana, a Philippine species closely related to P. schilleriana, has similar silver-mottled foliage but carries the distinction of white upper flowers giving way to lower petals and sepals heavily spotted with reddish-purple, all borne on a long, gracefully arching and often branching spike. A mature plant can produce well over a hundred flowers on a single well-branched inflorescence, making it a dramatic specimen once established. Keep humidity high and provide steady warmth, since this species resents cold drafts and abrupt temperature drops more than many other phalaenopsis.

planting.note: Mount on cork bark or pot in a small, well-drained clay pot with coarse bark; grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright light, since Dendrobium chrysotoxum cannot tolerate frost and needs a pronounced cool, dry winter rest to flower well.

directions: Grow in bright light with a few hours of gentle direct morning sun, in a small pot or mounted on cork bark, watering and feeding heavily during the summer growing season. Dendrobium chrysotoxum, native to the Himalayan foothills and Southeast Asia, produces short, clustered, spindle-shaped pseudobulbs each topped with a pendant raceme of fragrant, deep golden-yellow flowers with an orange-red blotch on the fringed lip in spring. This species requires a cool, distinctly dry rest through winter with minimal water once its canes mature and leaves drop, since continued warmth and moisture at that stage promote keiki growth instead of flower buds. Resume regular watering only as new roots and growths emerge in spring.

common_name: Fragrant Dendrobium (Pendulous Cane Orchid, Anosmum Orchid)

planting.note: Mount on a cork slab or hang in a basket with minimal coarse bark to accommodate its long pendulous canes; grow in bright light with a hard winter dry rest, since Dendrobium anosmum drops its leaves and cannot tolerate frost.

directions: Grow mounted or in a hanging basket in bright light, watering and fertilizing freely during the summer growing season while the long, pendulous canes elongate. Dendrobium anosmum, widespread from India through the Philippines, drops its leaves in the cool dry season and then bursts into bloom along the full length of its bare, cane-like pseudobulbs, producing large, intensely fragrant rosy-magenta flowers with a darker, velvety throat. A firm winter rest with sharply reduced water and cooler nights is essential to trigger this leafless bloom; premature watering once growth resumes tends to produce keikis along the cane instead of flowers. Once new growths and roots appear in spring, resume regular watering and begin light feeding.

common_name: Easter Orchid (Venezuela's National Flower, Flor de Mayo)

planting.note: Pot in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic orchid mix of bark and perlite in a clay pot that fits the root mass snugly; grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in bright light in zone 10, since Cattleya mossiae cannot tolerate frost.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light with a few hours of gentle direct sun in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix, letting the mix approach dryness between thorough waterings. Cattleya mossiae, the national flower of Venezuela, produces large, fragrant, 6–7-inch lavender-pink flowers with a ruffled, deep magenta and yellow-throated lip in late winter to spring, traditionally timed near Easter in its native cloud forests of the coastal cordillera. Give strong light for compact growth and abundant flowering, since plants grown in too much shade produce lush foliage but few blooms, and allow a brief cooler, drier rest after each growth matures. Its large, classic corsage-type flowers and reliable spring bloom have made it one of the most historically important species in Cattleya hybridizing.

planting.note: Pot in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic orchid mix in a clay pot sized to allow a couple of years' growth, since it forms dense clumps of tall pseudobulbs; grow in bright light in zone 10, since Cattleya bowringiana cannot tolerate frost.

directions: Grow in bright light with several hours of gentle direct sun in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix, watering freely and feeding during active summer growth. Cattleya bowringiana, native to Belize, Guatemala, and Honduras, forms tall, slender clumping pseudobulbs and in fall produces dense, rounded clusters of 8 to 15 or more medium-sized rose-purple flowers per spike, an unusually floriferous habit among large-flowered cattleyas. Its clustering growth habit, tolerance of strong light, and dependable autumn bloom make it one of the easiest and most rewarding cattleya species for beginning growers. Allow a modest cooler, drier rest after growths mature in late fall to help set the following year's flower buds.

common_name: Golden Shower Orchid (Dancing Lady Orchid, Varicosum Oncidium)

planting.note: Mount on cork bark or pot in a small, fast-draining epiphytic mix in a shallow clay pot; grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright light, since Oncidium varicosum cannot tolerate frost.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light with a little gentle morning sun in a small, fast-draining mix or mounted on cork, watering thoroughly and allowing the roots to dry somewhat between waterings. Oncidium varicosum, a Brazilian species, sends up tall, branching sprays in fall bearing dozens of bright golden-yellow flowers dominated by an oversized, rounded lip that gives the plant its dancing-lady appearance and common name. Reduce watering slightly and provide a modest cooler rest once new pseudobulbs mature in late summer to encourage the branching autumn flower spikes. Its compact growth and prolific, long-lasting sprays of color have made it a long-standing parent species in yellow-flowered oncidium-alliance hybrids.

planting.note: Pot in a fine, well-drained terrestrial orchid mix of fir bark, perlite, and charcoal in a small plastic pot; grow as a houseplant on a shaded windowsill, since Paphiopedilum sukhakulii cannot tolerate frost or direct sun.

directions: Grow in low to moderate light with no direct sun, in a fine, well-drained terrestrial mix kept lightly and evenly moist year-round without ever drying out completely. Paphiopedilum sukhakulii, discovered in Thailand in the 1960s, forms handsome fans of broad leaves mottled in two shades of green and sends up a single flower with a wide, apple-green dorsal sepal striped in dark maroon and long, spreading, warty green petals edged in deep purple-maroon spots. Unlike many slipper orchids it tolerates intermediate to warm household temperatures year-round without a distinct dry rest, making it a good candidate for growers without a cool greenhouse. Keep humidity moderate to high and feed lightly at quarter-strength with each watering, since this species has no pseudobulbs to store reserves.
